sources.airKgPerCubicMetre: Air at sea level in the International Standard Atmosphere, 15 °C
sources.referenceHeightMetres: The Beaufort scale, which our wind keeps, gives the wind at 10 m above the sea (WMO)
sources.gradientExponent: The wind over the open sea grows with height as (z/10 m)^0.11 (Hsu, Meindl & Gilhousen 1994, via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forces_on_sails)
sources.bluffDrag: A flat plate across the wind (NASA Glenn, Shape Effects on Drag, via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drag_coefficient): a hull's side and her furled rig, as the wind meets them
sources.line: The rig's lines are vanilla's rope, flax standing in for every plant fibre as the stake rope does (storms.json): its density, breaking load and stretch at break from config/vessels/materials.json, whose breaking load was measured on 12 mm rope (BS EN ISO 1181), scaled to each line's thickness by its cross-section. Its stretch rings out far faster than a tick, so each length of it stops at its rest stretched as its material and the tension let it, and it never pushes; the air drags it as a cylinder across the flow (C_d 1.2)
sources.crew: How fast her crew works her rig. walkMetresPerSecond: a person carrying the yard's heel along her, the normal walking speed of people on a rolling ship's deck, 1.28 to 1.68 m/s at the berth less 4 to 10% for the roll (Wang, Liu, Wang, Loughney, Yang and Gao 2020, Physica A 562, doi:10.1016/j.physa.2020.125369). haulMetresPerSecond: a line hauled or eased by hand, the rope-pulling speed at the lightest load measured, 1.87 m/s at 147.5 N (Arakawa et al. 2017, Sports Medicine International Open 1(4), doi:10.1055/s-0043-112335, a rope ergometer at maximal effort, the closest measured analogue): a sheet is worked with a turn round a beam (H&H 1:317), taking in what the sail gives, so the crew moves it at hand speed, not against its whole load
sources.camber: A full sail's depth over its chord: Marchaj's tunnel sails were cut to about 12% (AYRS 111, Rig Efficiency, Fig. 12)
sources.airMetresSquaredPerSecond: Air's kinematic viscosity at sea level in the International Standard Atmosphere, 15 °C. A sail's cloth drags the air along both its faces as a flat plate does, by the Reynolds number its chord and the wind make: 1.328 / √Re a face while the flow over it is laminar (Blasius), 0.074 Re^−0.2 once it is turbulent (Prandtl), changing at Re 5 × 10⁵
sources.flow: A sail is a thin wing of its cloth's outline as the wind meets it this tick: its span across the flow along the cloth and its chord along it. While the flow holds, it presses normal to the cloth by the leading-edge suction analogy, C_N = K_p sin α cos α + K_v sin² α (Polhamus, NASA TN D-3767, 1966), K_p and K_v from a vortex lattice on that outline: the lift slope, the leading edges' suction (thrust K_p − K_p² K_i over the secant of each edge's sweep, eq. 13) and the side edges' (Lamar, NASA TR R-428, 1974); on a 25° delta it gives K_v 3.2 as Polhamus did, on rectangles of aspect 0.5 to 2 Lamar's within 5%. Once the flow has left it, the cloth is a plate in separated flow: Rayleigh's free-streamline law, C_N ∝ sin α (4 + π) / (4 + π sin α), at the measured drag of a plate square across the wind, normalPlate: 1.11 + 0.02 (A + 1/A) (ESDU 70015, as Ortiz, Rival and Wood give it, Energies 8, 2015, eq. 3); with the plates they measured from aspect 0.4 to 9 it gives their normal force past the stall within a tenth. Where the flow breaks is measured: on an outline whose leading edge is swept vortexSweepDegrees or more, deltas, [sweep, the vortex burst at the trailing edge, at the apex] (Wentz and Kohlman, NASA CR-98737, 1969, Fig. 4.1.1, and Fig. 5.10.1 for 77.5°; read off the plots); on any other, plates, [1 / aspect, the normal force's peak, where it has fallen away] for flat rectangles (Winter, NACA TM 798, 1936, Fig. 3; read off the plot), and 9° for a plate of endless span (Fage and Johansen, as Ortiz et al. give it)
sources.clothKgPerSquareMetre: Experimental reconstructions of flax sails weigh 500 to 720 g/m² (Propylaeum, Heidelberg University, books.ub.uni-heidelberg.de/propylaeum/catalog/view/1035/1768/102856): a sail fills as the wind's pressure outweighs its cloth
